title: Bootkit
summary: A bootkit is malware that takes control of a system early in the boot process, before the operating system or its security software starts. It targets pre-operating-system code such as the master boot record on older systems, the bootloader, or UEFI firmware, and it may also install a malicious boot driver that loads at kernel start. Because it runs first, a bootkit can hide its own files and processes from the running system, weaken protections such as Secure Boot, and load further malware on every start. In a real environment it appears as unexplained boot changes, unexpected firmware settings, security agents that fail to load, or a system that stays compromised after a reinstall that does not touch the boot chain. The common mistake is treating a bootkit like ordinary file-based malware and expecting an operating system reinstall to clear it, when firmware or bootloader persistence survives that step; defenders therefore need boot integrity measurement and a full, verified firmware and disk rebuild rather than a quick cleanup.

beginner.definition: A bootkit is a type of malware that runs very early, before your operating system starts. It hides inside the part of the computer that begins the start-up process. Because it runs first, it can hide itself and control what loads next. This makes it much harder to find than normal viruses.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security tools start with the operating system, which is too late. A bootkit is already running by then, so it can hide its files and switch off protections. It can also come back every time you restart the machine. This means ordinary cleaning and even a simple reinstall may not remove it. You need to check the boot process itself.
howItWorks: You press the power button, and the firmware runs a short self-test of the hardware.
The firmware then finds a boot device and hands control to the boot code on it.
A bootkit changes that boot code or the firmware so its own code runs first.
The bootkit starts the real operating system but keeps control underneath it.
From that hidden position it can hide files, weaken protection, or load more malware.
Because it sits below the operating system, normal cleaning tools often cannot see it.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel with a front desk that greets every guest. The operating system is that front desk. A bootkit is someone who changes the guest list before the desk opens. Every guest is then sent to a room the stranger chooses. The desk staff behave normally and see nothing wrong. Even if you replace the desk staff, the changed list is still there. You must check the list itself, not just the people at the desk.
takeaways: A bootkit runs before your operating system, so it hides below your normal tools.
Turning on Secure Boot and keeping firmware updated helps block this kind of attack.
If you suspect one, get expert help and rebuild the machine from trusted media.

objectives: Explain what a bootkit is and why it runs before the operating system starts.
Describe where boot-level persistence lives, such as the master boot record, bootloader, or firmware.
Identify signs that a system may be compromised below the operating system.
Explain how Secure Boot and measured boot make boot-level tampering harder.
Describe why an ordinary reinstall may fail to remove a bootkit.
State the safe recovery steps for a suspected boot-level infection.
